title: At 91, 'Grey Beard' Reclaims His Appalachian Trail Record
summary:
Most people celebrate a 91st birthday with cake. Dale Sanders celebrated by finishing a 2,198-mile hike.

On August 31, 2026, the Memphis, Tennessee, native — nicknamed "Grey Beard" — became the oldest person to complete the Appalachian Trail. The AT stretches from Springer Mountain, Georgia, to Mount Katahdin, Maine, crossing forests, mountains, and rocky terrain. Only about a third of the 3,000-plus hikers who attempt it each year actually finish.

Sanders' trek took 359 days, just under the 365-day limit. He started at Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, near the trail's midpoint, because he wanted to see Georgia's fall leaves. To dodge the snow, he paused for winter, then resumed in spring and headed north.

He averaged about 12 miles a day with one rest day weekly. He also fell 71 times. In June, descending Vermont's Killington Mountain, he crashed into a boulder field, scraping his legs, arms, and hands. Weeks later, his left arm went numb, and doctors initially feared a stroke. Tests showed a pinched nerve instead. Exhausted, Sanders nearly quit with 140 miles left — but family and supporters urged him on.

Then, roughly 1,000 feet from Katahdin's summit, he lost his balance and fell onto the rocks. He lay there a moment, got up, and kept climbing.

Remarkably, this isn't his first time holding the title. He first set the record in 2017 at 82. His close friend M.J. "Sunny" Eberhart broke it in 2021 at 83 — and Sanders had encouraged her to do it. But after watching her succeed, he wanted the record back.

The AT is just one of his adventures: at 80, he canoed the entire Mississippi River; at 85, he hiked the Grand Canyon rim-to-rim-to-rim; at 87, he paddled the Mississippi again. His secret? Daily exercise and a positive attitude. "You just have to want to do it," he says.
why_it_matters: Age records like this one push back on assumptions about what older people can physically do, but they also raise real questions for sports, parks and rescue services about how much risk society should accept from very elderly adventurers chasing a title.

background_read: The Appalachian Trail (a 2,198-mile footpath running through 14 U.S. states from Georgia to Maine) is one of the country's best-known long-distance hikes, and it belongs to a group of three giant routes often called the 'Triple Crown' — the others are the Pacific Crest Trail and the Continental Divide Trail.

No single government agency runs it alone: the nonprofit Appalachian Trail Conservancy, founded in the 1920s, works with the National Park Service, the U.S. Forest Service, and thousands of volunteer maintainers. Its headquarters sits in Harpers Ferry, West Virginia (a small town near the trail's rough midpoint), which is why many long-distance hikers start or pause their trips there.

Katahdin (Maine's highest peak and the trail's northern end) is the finish line for northbound hikers, who usually start in Georgia in early spring to stay ahead of winter. Most people who set out never finish — injuries, money, and weather end many attempts — which is why only about a third of the thousands who try each year reach the end.

Earl Shaffer became the first person to hike the whole trail in one continuous trip in 1948, and 'thru-hiking' — completing the entire trail in a single journey — has grown into a culture of its own since then.

perspectives.description: Hikers and record-watchers see Sanders as proof that endurance sport does not have to end at 70 or 80. His 359-day trek, careful winter break and daily routine show that age records come from planning and habit, not luck, and his story may encourage other older people to stay active outdoors.

Some observers worry that chasing age records pushes elderly people into avoidable danger — 71 falls, a possible stroke scare and a tumble 1,000 feet from the summit are serious warning signs. They argue that the pressure to set a record can override good judgment and that rescue teams and families may end up paying the cost.

The 'oldest thru-hiker' title is informal rather than an official championship, and it has now changed hands repeatedly — 82, then 83, now 91 — as the population of retired, health-conscious long-distance hikers grows. That pattern reflects broader changes in longevity, gear and trail infrastructure rather than one extraordinary individual.

The next question is whether records like this keep falling, and what safety guidance, medical monitoring or trail rules might follow. If more very old hikers attempt full thru-hikes, trail organizations may need clearer advice on pacing, injuries and knowing when to stop.
